content: Write a LinkedIn post about what I learned from a project that failed.

Here's a draft. I've used brackets where you'll want to drop in real specifics — the concrete details are what make these posts land instead of reading like generic wisdom.

---

**Eighteen months ago I pitched [project]. Last [month], we shut it down.**

We were solving a problem that wasn't a problem.

Not for lack of effort. The team shipped on time, the tech worked, the demo was genuinely impressive. But we'd built the whole thing on an assumption we never seriously tested: that [customers would pay to solve X]. When we finally put it in front of real users, they were polite. Politeness is the worst signal you can get.

Three things I took away:

**Enthusiasm isn't validation.** Early conversations were full of "that's interesting" and "keep me posted." I read those as demand. They were manners.

**The expensive mistakes happen before you write any code.** We spent [X months] building and [two weeks] on discovery. That ratio should have been closer to reversed.

**Killing it sooner would have been the braver call.** I saw the warning signs around month [six] and talked myself out of them, because I'd already sold the vision internally and didn't want to be the person who changed their mind. Sunk cost is an ego problem as much as a finance one.

The project failed. I'd argue the team didn't — we know more about [our market] now than any competitor deck could have taught us.

What's the failure that taught you the most?

---

A few notes:

- **The closing question** is optional but it does drive comments if that's what you're after. Cut it if it feels like bait.
- **Name your own role in it.** The post works because you're taking responsibility, not narrating from a distance. Resist any urge to soften that in editing.
- **Check with your team and legal** before naming clients, revenue figures, or anything about why a specific deal died.

If you tell me the actual project, your industry, and what genuinely went wrong, I can rewrite this so it sounds like you rather than like a LinkedIn template.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

When the reader already knows the background, the post stops being a story and becomes a verdict. No setup, no reveal, no explaining what went wrong — they watched it go wrong. What they don't know is what you concluded, so that's the whole post now.

---

**[Project] is dead and most of you know why. Here's what I think it cost us, and what I think we bought.**

I'm not going to relitigate the timeline. You lived it.

What I keep coming back to is month [six]. That's when I had enough signal to call it and didn't. Not because the data was ambiguous — because I'd spent [the spring] selling this internally and couldn't figure out how to walk it back without torching my own credibility. So I protected the credibility and spent [nine more months] of your work to do it.

That's the actual failure. Everything downstream was competent execution of a decision I should have reversed.

Two things I'm taking into the next one:

The discovery-to-build ratio was indefensible, and I set it. [Two weeks] of customer conversations against [eighteen months] of engineering isn't a process failure, it's a priority I communicated by how I spent the calendar.

And I need people who will tell me I'm wrong in a way I can't reinterpret as enthusiasm. Several of you tried. I heard hedging where you meant no. That's on my listening, not your phrasing — but I'd rather we build the habit of being blunter than rely on me getting better at reading between lines.

The [market research / infrastructure / customer relationships] we came out with is real, and I'm not going to pretend the whole thing was waste. But it was an expensive way to learn it, and the price was mostly paid by people who weren't the ones who chose it.

---

Notes on this version:

- **It's riskier than the first draft.** Naming month six and taking public responsibility is the thing that makes it credible to people who were there — a vaguer version would read as spin, and they'd know. But if there's any active dispute about who decided what, or if leadership above you sees this as airing internal business, run it past someone first.
- **Watch for it landing as blame.** Lines like "several of you tried" are meant to credit people, but a reader who raised a flag and got overruled may read it as being volunteered into your redemption arc. Worth checking with one or two of them.
- **I cut the closing question.** Inviting an audience who lived the failure to share their own failures reads as tone-deaf.
- **Length:** this is close to the ceiling for a post where the reader has no story pulling them through. If you trim, cut the second takeaway before the first — the discovery-ratio point is the one that changes future behavior.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

---

**The failure wasn't [project]. It was month [six], when I had enough signal to stop and didn't.**

Not because the data was ambiguous. Because I'd spent [the spring] selling this internally and couldn't work out how to walk it back without torching my own credibility. So I protected the credibility and spent [nine more months] of your work doing it.

Everything after that was competent execution of a decision I should have reversed.

Two things I'm carrying forward. The discovery-to-build ratio was indefensible and I set it — [two weeks] of customer conversations against [eighteen months] of engineering is a priority you communicate with your calendar. And several of you flagged it in terms I heard as hedging. That's my listening, not your phrasing, but I'd rather we get blunter than rely on me reading between lines.

What we came out with is real. It was just an expensive way to learn it, and the price was mostly paid by people who didn't make the call.

---

Notes:

- **The lead now carries the whole post**, so month [six] and the credibility line are the two details worth getting exactly right. Everything else can flex.
- **If you need to go shorter still,** cut the discovery-ratio sentence. The listening point is the one your team can act on immediately.
- **The caveats from the last version still apply** — worth a check with the people you're referring to in that second takeaway, and with anyone above you if this is going somewhere public.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

---

**The failure wasn't [project]. It was month [six], when I had enough signal to stop and didn't.**

Not because the data was ambiguous. Because I'd spent [the spring] selling this internally and couldn't work out how to walk it back without torching my own credibility. So I protected the credibility and spent [nine more months] of your work doing it.

Everything after that was competent execution of a decision I should have reversed.

Two things I'm carrying forward. The discovery-to-build ratio was indefensible and I set it — [two weeks] of customer conversations against [eighteen months] of engineering is a priority you communicate with your calendar. And several of you flagged it in terms I heard as hedging. That's my listening, not your phrasing, but I'd rather we get blunter than rely on me reading between lines.

It was an expensive lesson, and the price was mostly paid by people who didn't make the call.

---

Notes:

- **What I cut:** "What we came out with is real." That was the only outcome claim in the piece. Removing it left "It was just an expensive way to learn it" with nothing to point back to, so I reworked that clause to stand alone. Everything else is untouched.
- **One thing to be aware of:** that line was the post's only upside, so the ending is now unrelieved. For a team audience that read the previous draft, this may land colder than you intend. If you want to soften it without making a results claim, something forward-looking about the next project would do it — happy to draft that if useful.
